The Song

The Battle of New Orleans

Written by Jimmy Driftwood  ·  Sung by Johnny Horton  ·  1959

The Battle of New Orleans

Words & music by Jimmy Driftwood  ·  As recorded by Johnny Horton

★

Verse One

In 1814 we took a little trip
Along with Colonel Jackson down the mighty Mississip’
We took a little bacon and we took a little beans
And we caught the bloody British in a town in New Orleans

Verse Two

We fired our cannon ’til the barrel melted down
So we grabbed an alligator and we fought another round
We filled his head with cannonballs, ’n’ powdered his behind
And when we touched the powder off, the gator lost his mind

Chorus

We fired our guns and the British kept a-comin’
There wasn’t nigh as many as there was a while ago
We fired once more and they began to runnin’
On down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico

Verse Three

We looked down the river and we see’d the British come
And there must have been a hundred of ’em beatin’ on the drum
They stepped so high and they made their bugles ring
We stood beside our cotton bales and didn’t say a thing

— Chorus —

Verse Four

Old Hickory said we could take ’em by surprise
If we didn’t fire our muskets ’til we looked ’em in the eye
We held our fire ’til we see’d their faces well
Then we opened up with squirrel guns and really gave ’em hell

Final Chorus

We fired our guns and the British kept a-comin’
There wasn’t nigh as many as there was a while ago
We fired once more and they began to runnin’
On down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico

Yeah, they ran through the briars and they ran through the brambles
And they ran through the bushes where a rabbit couldn’t go
They ran so fast that the hounds couldn’t catch ’em
On down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico

Written by Jimmy Driftwood (James Corbitt Morris). Recorded by Johnny Horton, 1959.

Melody from the traditional fiddle tune “The Eighth of January.”

The Story Behind the Song

A schoolteacher’s history lesson, set to an old fiddle tune, became one of the biggest records in America.

The Battle — January 8, 1815

In the last great battle of the War of 1812, Major General Andrew Jackson’s ragtag force — regulars, Tennessee and Kentucky riflemen, Creole militia, free men of color, Choctaw warriors, and even Jean Lafitte’s Baratarian pirates — stood behind cotton bales and an earthwork line at Chalmette, just downriver from New Orleans.

The British assault columns were cut down in the open field, and their commander, Major General Sir Edward Pakenham, was killed. The battle was over in about half an hour. Neither side yet knew the peace treaty had been signed at Ghent on Christmas Eve, two weeks before — the news had not yet crossed the Atlantic.

The Schoolteacher — Jimmy Driftwood

James Corbitt Morris, who performed as Jimmy Driftwood, was an Arkansas schoolteacher and principal with a gift for putting history to music. He wrote “The Battle of New Orleans” to hold his students’ attention, setting his words to “The Eighth of January,” a fiddle tune named for the date of Jackson’s victory and long played at dances across the South.

The Hit — Johnny Horton, 1959

Johnny Horton’s recording carried the song far beyond the classroom. Released in 1959, it climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, held the top spot for six weeks, and became a Grammy Award–winning record — a history lesson America could not stop singing.

Sheet prepared November 18, 2026.
